purpose: Design-only appraisal of published evidence, its scope, access and reuse. No participant-level analyses, transcript extraction, clinical ratings or submissions.

primary_clinical_anchor.citation: Zimmerer V, Tsoukala A, Çokal D, et al. The relationship between language disorder and thought disorder: Comparing micro- and macrostructure of spoken narratives of people with aphasia and people with schizophrenia. Cortex 195 (2026) 81–95. Online 2025-12-31.
primary_clinical_anchor.design: One eight-frame near-wordless Dinner Party cartoon; spoken English; all native English speakers. 30 people with schizophrenia and 15 comparison controls in Newcastle plus 20 people with aphasia and 30 controls in London; different clinical groups have separate controls.
primary_clinical_anchor.observations_in_paper: More severe conceptual disorganization within the schizophrenia sample was associated with more narrative misdescriptions (Spearman rho .51, p .003 as printed) and lower evaluative devices (rho −.61, p < .001); Section 3.4. Table 3 defines denominators. The authors label correlation analyses exploratory.
primary_clinical_anchor.scope: A broad source category counts wrong, odd or irrelevant descriptions. The proposed E only counts clearly contradicted propositions. The source combines within-group standardized qualitative/emotional expression rates; proposed V is a raw nonduplicated span density. Only the direction of the two prespecified contrasts can be compared. An individual participant need not exhibit both features. No equivalent diagnosis score assigned to models.
primary_clinical_anchor.license: Article explicitly CC BY 4.0. Cite source when summarizing published statistics. Rights to the original Fletcher & Birt cartoon, separate data files and external model processing were not established by the article license.

primary_data_access.csv_access: Public partial byte-range request HTTP 206; first header line inspected. No participant rows printed, extracted for analysis or delivered.
primary_data_access.data_type: Speaker-level derived features and clinical measures; no transcript field. Codebook defines JointSZ as four clinical/control groups and Disorganization as the PANSS conceptual disorganization question. Published primary within-SZ results are continuous rank associations; no FTD high/low grouping was required or assumed for the proposed test.
primary_data_access.zip_checked: Listed entries and read variable definitions and already-computed results in Within_Group_Correlations_R_analysis.Rmd / .html. No standalone license was listed in this zip. Pair rows 51 and 56 in the schizophrenia section show evaluative devices rho −0.608443559, raw p .000461890, FDR p .00461890 and misdescriptions rho .511393706, raw p .003873328, FDR p .02582219. Raw p for misdescriptions differs slightly from the printed paper. No statistics recomputed on individual data.
primary_data_access.pdf_status: Separate model-summary PDF was present in the public index; its contents were not needed to design the study.
primary_data_access.usage: Only the published findings and definitions are on the critical path. File-level reuse, redistribution, and exposure to an external model were not established. No patient files included in the project's deliverables.

comparison_sources.citation: Achim AM, Achim A, Fossard M (2022). Referential communication in people with recent-onset schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
comparison_sources.verified: Full paper and data statement. French-speaking setting. 25 recent-onset spectrum outpatients (17 schizophrenia) and 25 controls recruited; character identification in a real interaction. Group-by-likely-knowledge interaction for the quantity of spontaneous information, p .049. Within-SZ association with theory of mind not significant. Publication offers raw data from the authors; no public unrestricted participant corpus acquired.
comparison_sources.role: Alternative based on addressee adaptation; not a validation of the proposed history cue.

comparison_sources.citation: Achim et al. Use of reference markers in the speech of people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders: Evidence from two referential communication tasks manipulating common ground with the interaction partner.
comparison_sources.verified: Institutional full text. Results vary by reference type, task and first vs subsequent mention. In general the two groups both showed sensitivity to likely knowledge. Raw data available on request.
comparison_sources.role: Counterevidence to treating common-ground sensitivity as uniformly absent.

comparison_sources.citation: Barch DM, Berenbaum H (1997). The effect of language production manipulations on negative thought disorder and discourse coherence disturbances in schizophrenia.
comparison_sources.verified: Abstract. Thirty-nine participants with schizophrenia answered questions after stories. Unstructured questions yielded more discourse coherence disturbances than structured ones. No speech dataset or reuse license inspected.
comparison_sources.role: Alternative structured-question/discourse-goal design; not evidence for the two primary outcomes.

comparison_sources.citation: Hoffman RE et al. (2011). Using computational patients to evaluate illness mechanisms in schizophrenia.
comparison_sources.verified: Published methods and findings on delayed story recall, 37 schizophrenia/schizoaffective outpatients and 20 controls; agent-slotting errors and derailment compared with a computational model. No reusable participant archive established.
comparison_sources.role: Alternative constrained role-binding design, not a memory mechanism replication using subscription CLI.

comparison_sources.citation: Çokal D et al. (2018). The language profile of formal thought disorder.
comparison_sources.verified: Full paper. English cartoon narration, 15 SZ+FTD, 15 SZ−FTD, 15 nonclinical controls, 15 first-degree relatives. Subgroups formed using PANSS conceptual disorganization item. More definite NP use in the low-FTD group was descriptive in corrected pairwise comparisons; group-model results differ by analysis. No patient transcript used.
comparison_sources.role: Alternative referential-NP measure and evidence of heterogeneity.

comparison_sources.citation: Çokal D et al. (2026). Automated detection of referential features in schizophrenic speech using large language models.
comparison_sources.verified: Full article. Reuses an existing manually coded English dataset. NP type extraction differs by method and is not clinical validation of generated language. Data statement describes ethical/privacy restrictions and reasonable request. Review-only link not used.
comparison_sources.role: Precedent for measuring specific textual features; no raw participant data used.

comparison_sources.citation: Fradkin I, Nour MM, Dolan RJ (2023). Theory-Driven Analysis of Natural Language Processing Measures of Thought Disorder Using Generative Language Modeling.
comparison_sources.verified: Full article CC BY; GPT-2 temperature and memory-span perturbations; 2 blinded clinicians rated 249 synthetic narratives. Public API root inventory spans 2 pages (11 entries); Results inventory returned 11 plotting and results files. No explicitly named raw clinician-score file in these listings. Script download followed a redirect to an unresolved storage hostname; CSV contents and possible embedded clinician scores not verified. Project metadata had no node_license. No embedding/model files downloaded.
comparison_sources.role: Alternative generative method; neither its parameter manipulation nor its clinician judgment can be transferred to this study.

comparison_sources.citation: Mota NB et al. (2012). Speech Graphs Provide a Quantitative Measure of Thought Disorder in Psychosis.
comparison_sources.verified: Primary paper and supplement descriptions. Portuguese dream-report task, eight participants per group. Table S3 lists derived speech-graph attributes and clinical scale results. This is not a validated English picture-narration benchmark; no participant file used.
